title: WendigoActionPlan
description: One complete engagement for the wendigo: where it positions itself, what it does, and where it withdraws to afterward. The wendigo is a persistent presence, not something that spawns fresh each time - it's usually already nearby, quietly keeping its distance, before this plan ever runs; spawn_at is where it moves to (walking there if not already close - or not moving at all if it's already at a good distance for what the plan is about to do - appearing fresh only for a genuine first encounter) before 'plan' starts, not a guaranteed brand-new appearance every request. Positioning throughout this whole plan works the same way: everywhere a distance band is named (spawn_at, movement.approach_band, despawn_band), it's resolved LIVE, fresh, against wherever the player actually is at that exact moment - never a position frozen from earlier in the request. combat.break_torch has no band of its own - it always targets the nearest torch to wherever the wendigo itself currently is. This one call drives the entire engagement start to finish - there is no mid-engagement re-planning, so 'plan' should account for how the target might react (e.g. predicate.player_unreachable, predicate.player_looking_at_self) rather than assuming a fresh decision partway through. The prompt accompanying this schema describes the target player, their dweller severity, the live band distance-from-player ladder, and how many torches currently sit at each band - that context is NOT part of this schema since it's different every request. Where the wendigo withdraws to afterward IS a model choice (see despawn_band) - the engine resolves a live position in that band at the moment it's actually time to flee, re-resolving fresh if the first attempt fails; this is a retreat back into hiding, not vanishing from existence, unless it genuinely can't find anywhere dark to go. The model is never asked for raw coordinates, exact tick counts, or arbitrary speed floats - those are all engine-side lookups from semantic enums, and predicates are likewise engine-evaluated facts, not expressions the model computes itself. 'global_rules' back hard requirements that must hold no matter which plan step is currently running (see its own description) - use those for anything non-negotiable; use control.if/control.while inside 'plan' for everything else.

previous_encounter_recap.description: Write this FIRST, before deciding spawn_at/plan below - your own one-sentence, in-character narrative interpretation of what actually happened during the wendigo's most recent encounter with this player, using the prompt's own factual account of it (never caught them, caught them but they got away before any damage landed, or caught them and dealt damage before it ended - three genuinely different outcomes, not one binary caught/not-caught fact - was spotted dead-on or never directly stared at, vanished unnoticed or had to withdraw/flee, how many torches it broke, whether the engine had to cut the encounter short - lost track of them, they went out of reach, or something else forced an early stop, as opposed to a clean ending - and the plan's own shape - e.g. posture.stare then combat.break_torch). Don't just restate those facts mechanically - interpret them as a horror beat, the way a viewer would describe what they just watched: e.g. 'I set a stare jumpscare, but the player never looked - I wasn't seen, the reveal fizzled' or 'Stared until they noticed, then broke a torch right in front of them and vanished before they could react' or 'Lost them mid-chase after they broke away - I'll need to close faster next time.' This sentence becomes YOUR OWN memory of that encounter - it's shown back to you verbatim (as 'what happened last time,' replacing this same factual account) the next time you're asked to plan for this player, so use it to actually pace the story: don't repeat a beat that already landed, build on tension that hasn't paid off yet, or ease up after a string of failed attempts, the way a real haunting would escalate or vary rather than looping the same scare. Empty string if this is the wendigo's first encounter with this player this session (nothing to recap yet) - never invent a past encounter that didn't happen.

plan.description: Runs after spawning, before the despawn move. Executed in order. If a step's precondition isn't met (e.g. retreat_to_dark with source=stored but nothing has been stored yet), the engine falls back to a sensible default rather than erroring - it never rejects a whole plan for one bad step.

despawn_band.description: Which live distance band from the player the wendigo withdraws to once 'plan' finishes (or whenever a movement.retreat_with_fallback step runs) - resolved fresh at that moment, re-resolved again from wherever it actually ended up if the first attempt fails. This is a genuine choice, not always the maximum distance: a wendigo that just had a fleeting, subtle encounter might only need to back off to medium before resuming its quiet watch, while one that just committed to a chase or a grab plausibly wants real distance (farther/farthest) before showing itself again. medium is the closest option offered - deliberately no closer band exists here, since retreating any nearer than that isn't a real withdrawal. Independent of spawn_at's own severity-gated unlock ladder - all four options are always available regardless of severity, since choosing to retreat modestly rather than maximally is never the bold/risky half of a decision.

global_rules.description: Hard requirements the engine enforces every tick, independent of whatever 'plan' step is currently running or how deep inside a control.if/control.while it is - not a suggestion the model has to remember to re-check at every step. Each rule fires at most once per wave: the instant its condition becomes true, the engine stops whatever the wendigo is currently doing (interrupting mid-movement if needed) and runs its action immediately, then the plan resumes from wherever it left off once that action finishes (unless the action was control.despawn, which ends the wave outright). Use this for things that must never be allowed to happen regardless of which branch the model chose earlier - e.g. a rule with condition predicate.player_looking_at_self(band=dead_stare) and action control.despawn, so a dead-on stare ends the encounter immediately no matter what movement/posture step happens to be running at that moment, instead of relying on every single plan step remembering to check for it. Don't use this for ordinary reactive branching (e.g. 'wait until the player looks away before approaching') - that belongs in control.if/control.while inside 'plan', where the timing of the check is meant to matter. Empty array if nothing needs this level of enforcement for this wave.

step.description: Top-level plan entries: any primitive action, or a control.if/control.while wrapping a nested block of primitive actions. Control steps cannot nest inside each other (see action_step) - that keeps a plan at most two levels deep, which is what both the grammar-constrained decoder and a small model can reliably produce.

action_step.description: A primitive action - the only kind of step allowed inside a control.if/control.while block, so branches/loop bodies can't themselves contain more control flow.

movement_approach.description: MOVEMENT branch: close distance toward the player using vanilla pathfinding.

speed.description: Semantic pace, not a raw multiplier - engine maps each value to a fixed speed constant.

movement_approach_band.description: MOVEMENT branch: pathfind to a live position at the given distance band from the player - resolved fresh at the moment this step actually runs, against wherever the player is by then, never a position decided earlier in the plan. Only bands actually offered in the prompt are valid for this request (same severity/cave-scale gating as spawn_at). If the wendigo's current live distance already roughly fits what comes next, this step can simply be omitted - there's no requirement to move at all before an action if the current position already works.

band.description: Which live distance band to move to, relative to the player right now. 'no_players_looking' is a special value instead of naming a distance band (same meaning as spawn_at's own): pathfind from wherever the wendigo currently is to a live position roughly at the farther band that the player isn't currently facing toward, always available regardless of severity. Especially useful as the very first step of a plan that's engaging an entity already orbiting nearby - unlike a fresh spawn, an already-alive entity doesn't get repositioned by spawn_at at all, so this is how to explicitly walk it somewhere unwatched before the rest of the plan runs, the same way a fresh spawn_at=no_players_looking would. 'spot_above' (60%+ only, same meaning as spawn_at's own) - pathfind to the ceiling directly above the player, staying dark the whole way, settling for the closest reachable spot if light blocks a clean route straight above. Mid-plan repositioning onto the ceiling for a movement.drop, not just a fresh spawn choice - e.g. an already-orbiting entity moving into position for an overhead ambush.

speed.description: Semantic pace, not a raw multiplier - engine maps each value to a fixed speed constant.

movement_retreat_to_dark.description: MOVEMENT branch: move toward a dark location instead of the player.

source.description: 'stored' = pathfind to the location remembered by the most recent memory.store_dark_location step (falls back to scan_now if nothing is stored). 'scan_now' = scan the surroundings immediately and move there.

speed.description: Semantic pace, not a raw multiplier - engine maps each value to a fixed speed constant. A calm withdrawal reads differently from a startled flee - pick deliberately.

movement_retreat_with_fallback.description: MOVEMENT branch: retreat to a dark spot with the same robustness as the automatic despawn move - tries the wave's other scanned dark spots in order if the first attempt fails (stuck/unreachable/times out), then a fresh live scan as a last resort, before giving up. Prefer this over retreat_to_dark right after combat.lunge_attack, where reliably getting back into hiding matters more than a single best-effort attempt.

speed.description: Semantic pace, not a raw multiplier - engine maps each value to a fixed speed constant. Applies to every candidate this step tries, including fallback attempts.

movement_reposition.description: MOVEMENT branch: short-range tactical movement relative to a reference point - never absolute coordinates.

reference.description: What the direction/distance below are relative to.

distance.description: Semantic distance band - engine maps to a block-count range, not an exact value.

speed.description: Semantic pace, not a raw multiplier - engine maps each value to a fixed speed constant.

movement_hold.description: MOVEMENT branch: stop moving and hold the current position.

movement_drop.description: MOVEMENT branch: reserved for the same tier as combat.lunge_attack (60%+) - literally just releases whatever wall/ceiling attachment the wendigo currently has, nothing more. Not a targeted attack by itself and has no destination - if it's on the ceiling above the player when this runs, gravity does the rest; if it's not near the player at all, this just drops it straight down wherever it happens to be. Resolves the instant it's triggered, same as posture.stare or combat.teleport_to_band - the actual fall plays out physically over the next moment regardless of what the plan does right after. Safe to reach for anywhere in a plan, not just right after a deliberate spot_above positioning - if it's already resting on a floor (not attached to any wall/ceiling) when this runs, it's a real no-op, nothing happens, so there's no need to be certain a wall/ceiling attachment is still in effect by the time a later step actually executes. Works well in plenty of shapes beyond the classic spot_above setup: e.g. posture.stare from wherever it currently is, then movement.drop, then combat.chase - letting go mid-stare rather than only ever as a scripted overhead ambush. Pair with spawn_at/movement.approach_band(spot_above) beforehand for the deliberate overhead-ambush version, and combat.lunge_attack or combat.chase right after (either version) to actually close on and catch the player once it lands near them - the three are independent primitives, not one combined action, so mix them with whatever else fits the moment.

memory_store_dark_location.description: MEMORY branch: scan nearby and remember the darkest valid position for a later movement.retreat_to_dark(source=stored). Overwrites whatever was previously stored.

search_radius.description: Semantic scan radius - engine maps to a block range.

global_rule.description: One always-checked condition/action pair - see 'global_rules' at the top level for the full explanation of when this runs and why it's different from control.if/control.while.

posture_stare.description: POSTURE branch: toggle the glowing-eyes stare cue (existing setStaring hook). This step itself doesn't wait - the very next step in the plan starts resolving immediately, the same tick. The engine enforces a floor on top of that though: every enabled=true that begins a fresh stare (wasn't already staring) keeps the stare visually held for at least 3 real seconds no matter what the rest of the plan does immediately after - nothing to plan around, just don't expect an immediate follow-on step to actually take effect right away. That floor alone is NOT a substitute for a real stare-and-react beat, though: for anything longer, or to actually react to whether the player notices, follow this with a control.while loop whose condition is a predicate.player_looking_at_self or predicate.player_distance check (see control.while's own description for a worked example) - the extra wait/hold time beyond the floor comes entirely from that loop.

timing_wait.description: TIMING branch: pause before the next step in the plan executes.

duration.description: Engine maps this to a tick range (with light randomization) rather than an exact count, so identical plans don't feel mechanically identical. very_long is a real 'go dormant for a stretch' option (~20-30 real seconds) above long's own ceiling - reach for it when the plan wants the wendigo to sit still and let a long silence build, not just a slightly longer ordinary pause.

sound_ambient_cue.description: SOUND branch: plays a cue audible near the wendigo's current position, drawn from a distinct pool of cave sounds per cue. Heavily encouraged at the moment each cue is meant for (see below) - a plan is never required to include one, but it reads noticeably more alive when it does.

cue.description: chase = heavily encouraged right before committing to combat.lunge_attack or combat.chase - announces the hunt is on. flee = heavily encouraged right before movement.retreat_with_fallback - announces the withdrawal back into darkness. stare = heavily encouraged right when posture.stare(enabled=true) starts a held stare. ambient = a low, unplaced presence cue with no specific moment it needs to pair with - safe to use anytime, including from a distance.

sound_breathe.description: SOUND branch: a single, deliberate breathing sound, played right at the wendigo's own real position (audible to every player, not just whoever's closest) rather than the unplaced dread cues sound.ambient_cue uses. Available at every stage, including the very first, faintest one - get as close as possible to the target before using it; the closer it is when this plays, the more it reads as genuinely, physically there right beside them rather than a distant noise. Reach for it right after a close instant reposition - combat.teleport_to_band(band=close/behind_player), an ordinary close approach, or (once unlocked) band=above_player - and again right before escalating into whatever comes next for the current stage (movement.retreat_with_fallback/control.despawn early on, combat.lunge_attack/combat.chase/another teleport once those unlock). No parameters beyond 'type' - unlike sound.ambient_cue, there's only the one sound here, nothing to choose between.

combat_lunge_attack.description: COMBAT branch: a direct approach to melee range - one of the few movement primitives that's allowed to cross into light, since closing the distance is the point. Always closes at the fastest pace, not a semantic choice like other movement (no 'speed' field here) - a lunge is a commit-to-the-grab moment. On contact this doesn't deal damage directly - it grabs the player, forcing them to ride along with the wendigo until they either struggle free or the wendigo reaches wherever it's headed next (typically its despawn point), at which point it's their loss to make. Don't run this blind - use predicate.player_distance (closer_than lunge_distance) in a control.if/control.while to decide when the player is close enough to commit, since once started it commits to closing the remaining distance. Follow up with movement.retreat_with_fallback to get back into hiding afterward - the grabbed player rides along for that too. The engine also requires a dark-enough spot near the player before this will run at all (how near scales up with severity) - if the player is standing somewhere too brightly lit with nothing dark nearby to retreat to, this is a no-op and the plan continues, same as combat.break_torch finding no torch.

combat_break_torch.description: COMBAT branch: destroy a torch, snuffing that light out - like combat.lunge_attack, this is allowed to cross into light since reaching the target is the point. Always targets the single nearest known light source live from wherever the wendigo itself currently is (no positioning needed first, no band choice - picking a torch by its distance from the PLAYER instead used to send the wendigo straight through the lit area around them just to reach one on the far side, exactly the exposure this creature is supposed to avoid). If no torch is found nearby this is a no-op and the plan continues, never fails outright. A good sequence: spawn near a torch, break_torch, then movement.retreat_with_fallback to withdraw before despawning.

speed.description: Semantic pace, not a raw multiplier - engine maps each value to a fixed speed constant.

combat_chase.description: COMBAT branch: sustained, aggressive pursuit - reserved for the most aggressive tier (the engine won't allow this below 80%). Always runs at the fastest pace, not a semantic choice like other movement (no 'speed' field here). Should almost always be preceded by a posture.stare - this is the payoff for being noticed while staring, not something to trigger with no reveal moment first. Like combat.lunge_attack, catching the player here doesn't deal damage directly - it grabs them, forcing them to ride along until they struggle free or the wendigo reaches wherever it's headed next, ending the chase there rather than sustaining it further. Until it catches them, it passively destroys any torch within 10 blocks of wherever the wendigo currently is as it runs through - incidental collateral from the chase itself, not a targeted break_torch (no pathing to torches, no aiming for them specifically). Also ends on its own (without ever catching them) once the player can't be reached for a sustained stretch, at which point the plan simply continues to whatever comes next (typically the automatic despawn phase if nothing else follows) - no explicit flee/despawn step is required right after this one, though adding movement.retreat_with_fallback afterward is fine too. A good use: pair with a global_rule (condition predicate.player_looking_at_self at whichever band, action combat.chase) so being spotted at this tier immediately and reliably escalates into a real chase, regardless of what the current plan step was doing.

combat_teleport_to_band.description: COMBAT branch: instantly relocates the wendigo to a live-resolved spot at the given band, no travel time, no warning - a teleport, not a movement primitive, so it resolves the same instant it runs, nothing to wait on afterward. Every destination except band=torch must be completely unlit (0 light level, not merely dim) - torch is the one deliberate exception, since landing at a live light source can never itself read as unlit. Always available at every stage, unlike most of this creature's other combat options - the real gating here is which band value(s) are even offered right now (see 'band' below - the offered set GROWS with stage, cumulative, not replaced: everything unlocked at an earlier stage stays available at every later one too, alongside whatever's new) and a SEPARATE engine-enforced precondition this schema can't show directly: the wendigo can only actually pull this off while ITS OWN current live distance from the player already sits in one of the bands unlocked so far this stage (roughly the inverse of the destination progression, also cumulative - an early-stage wendigo can only blink away while already right on top of the player, a late-stage one has a much wider set of positions it can pull this off from). If that precondition isn't met right now, this is a clean no-op and the plan just continues - never a hard failure. If the chosen band itself can't be live-resolved (nothing fully unlit/valid found there, or no torch nearby for band=torch), the engine automatically falls back to the next best-to-worst option instead of failing outright - the full order, best to worst, is above_player, behind_player, torch, close, medium, far, farther, farthest, so a failed close attempt quietly becomes a medium teleport rather than nothing happening at all; only genuinely offer a band this schema is currently letting you pick, the engine handles the rest of the degradation on its own. Reach for this specifically when the player is sprinting AND the prompt's own account of the wendigo's current distance/band suggests the precondition is likely met - ideally as the very FIRST step of the plan, teleporting straight into position rather than pathing there normally, since a sprinting player is exactly the moment a sudden, silent reposition reads as unsettling rather than redundant. Pair with combat.lunge_attack, combat.chase, or posture.stare right after landing - band=torch specifically should almost always be followed by one of those, not left as the whole beat on its own, since arriving already exposed at a torch only reads as deliberate if something follows it up.

band.description: Which destination this teleport resolves to - the set of values actually offered grows with stage (cumulative: everything unlocked earlier stays available later too, alongside whatever's new that stage), never shrinks or replaces. farthest/farther/far/medium/close are the ordinary live-resolved positioning bands (same distance ranges as movement.approach_band), completely unlit (0 light level) but not necessarily unwatched. close and behind_player both specifically resolve to a completely unlit spot the player ISN'T currently looking toward - behind_player is the classic blind-spot ambush (right in their blind spot, the original version of this ability); close is the same idea from a slightly less point-blank range. above_player resolves to a ceiling attachment point directly (or as close to directly) above the player, 10-30 blocks straight up - a drop-in vantage rather than a ground-level appearance, also completely unlit. torch resolves to the single nearest live torch to the player - the one destination NOT required to be unlit (it's a light source by definition) - just a relocation, no side effect on the torch itself (it isn't destroyed and this doesn't start a chase on its own, unlike how spawning on a torch used to work) - the model decides separately whether to follow up with combat.break_torch, combat.lunge_attack, or combat.chase from there (see this action's own top-level description - a torch teleport with no follow-up reads as pointless, always pair it with something).

combat_teleport_in_view.description: COMBAT branch: instantly relocates the wendigo to a live-resolved spot at the given band, same no-travel-time mechanic as combat.teleport_to_band, but the resolved spot is one the player CAN currently see (in view), not one they're blind to - the deliberate opposite of that ability's own close/behind_player values. The spot is still required to be completely unlit (0 light level) even though it's in view - a visible silhouette in the dark, not a lit-up reveal. Meant for a reveal: teleport in, then let yourself be seen doing something specific rather than just noticed standing somewhere. Early stages, pair it with an immediate posture.stare right after landing - the reveal-and-stare read of this creature. Later stages, pair it with a stare that quickly turns into combat.chase or combat.lunge_attack (directly, or via a global_rule on predicate.player_looking_at_self) - the stare becomes the wind-up for the strike rather than the whole beat. Always available as an action type, same as combat.teleport_to_band - the offered band(s) grow with stage (see 'band' below), cumulative like that ability's own bands, EXCEPT stage 1 specifically gets every band at once (a deliberate exception - see 'band' below), not just the farthest one the ordinary progression would otherwise give it alone. No separate source-band precondition here, unlike combat.teleport_to_band - this reveal is meant to be pullable off from wherever the wendigo currently is. If nothing in-view/unlit is live-resolvable at the requested band, the engine automatically searches outward (progressively farther bands) instead of failing outright, so only ever pick one of the bands this schema is currently offering and let the engine handle the rest.

band.description: Which distance band this in-view teleport resolves to. Grows with stage like combat.teleport_to_band's own bands (farthest unlocks at stage 1, farther adds at stage 2, far at stage 3, medium at stage 4, close at stage 5 - each stage keeps everything from before too), with one deliberate exception: stage 1 alone is offered every band at once (farthest through close), not just farthest - a one-time allowance so even the very first, most cautious stage has real variety in how far away its single reveal-and-vanish beat happens, rather than always the identical distance. Unlike combat.teleport_to_band's bands, the resolved spot is always one the player can currently see, never a blind spot.

combat_teleport_to_eyeline.description: COMBAT branch: instantly relocates the wendigo to a live-resolved spot at the given band, same no-travel-time mechanic as combat.teleport_to_band/combat.teleport_in_view, but the resolved spot is BOTH completely unlit (0 light level, like every other teleport destination) AND genuinely inline with the player's current eyeline - not merely somewhere broadly in their field of view the way combat.teleport_in_view's own spots are, a tight, dead-on alignment with wherever they're actually looking right now. Meant for the most unsettling version of a reveal: something dark, barely visible, already sitting exactly where their gaze already rests, so the moment of being noticed feels like it was already waiting for them rather than announcing itself. Pair it the same way combat.teleport_in_view recommends - an immediate posture.stare right after landing early on, or a stare that turns straight into combat.chase/combat.lunge_attack at later stages. Always available as an action type at every stage, no separate source-band precondition (pullable off from wherever the wendigo currently is, same as combat.teleport_in_view) - the offered band(s) grow with stage (see 'band' below), cumulative, EXCEPT stage 1 specifically gets every band at once, same one-time exception combat.teleport_in_view's own stage 1 gets. If nothing unlit-and-inline-with-eyeline is live-resolvable at the requested band, the engine automatically searches outward (progressively farther bands) instead of failing outright, so only ever pick one of the bands this schema is currently offering and let the engine handle the rest.

band.description: Which distance band this eyeline teleport resolves to. Grows with stage exactly like combat.teleport_in_view's own band field (farthest unlocks at stage 1, farther adds at stage 2, far at stage 3, medium at stage 4, close at stage 5 - each stage keeps everything from before too), with the same one deliberate exception: stage 1 alone is offered every band at once (farthest through close), not just farthest. Unlike combat.teleport_in_view's bands (broadly in view), the resolved spot is always dark AND tightly aligned with the player's current gaze.

combat_teleport_ahead.description: COMBAT branch: instantly relocates the wendigo to a live-predicted spot along the player's own path, rather than a fixed band around wherever they currently stand - the closest thing this creature has to actually anticipating where the player is going, not just reacting to where they are right now. If the player is currently moving, the engine extrapolates a point some distance ahead along their live horizontal movement direction, then searches near THAT point for a landing spot - deliberately DIM (faintly lit, not pitch black) rather than the usual fully-dark requirement, since a player is far more likely to actually be walking through or near their own placed light than through genuine total darkness; landing somewhere dim near their predicted route reads as lying in wait along their real path, not teleporting to a random dark pocket that happens to be nearby but off their way. No band parameter - it always searches a fixed radius around the predicted point, not a distance-from-player band. If the player isn't currently moving, or nothing suitably dim turns up near the prediction, the engine automatically falls back to an ordinary combat.teleport_in_view instead (no failure state to plan around - this always resolves to SOME placement). Meant for a genuine ambush-in-wait: land ahead of them, then either posture.stare and hold (a control.while on predicate.player_approaching, letting the distance actually close before reacting) or let a held stare turn into combat.chase/combat.lunge_attack once they're close enough - waiting for them to arrive reads as far more unsettling than immediately closing the distance yourself. Always available as an action type, every stage.

control_none.description: CONTROL branch: explicit do-nothing step. Lets the model choose inaction deliberately instead of being forced to always act.

control_despawn.description: CONTROL branch: end this engagement immediately by vanishing right where the wendigo currently stands - no travel to a hiding spot first, no walk-away transition. Ends the plan the instant this step runs, so put it last. It still retreats into darkness and keeps watching from a distance afterward, same as any other ending - this only changes whether that withdrawal is instant or visible. Use this for a fleeting, passive presence: appear, do something small and unsettling from a distance, then simply not be there anymore - a much subtler beat than being watched fleeing into the dark. Not the same as movement.retreat_with_fallback (a real flight back into darkness, for when the wendigo needs to physically get away first) - if the wendigo isn't already somewhere fine to vanish from, retreat before using this.

control_re_evaluate.description: CONTROL branch: end the current plan right here and ask for a brand new one to replace everything after this point - available at any severity, any point in the plan (top-level, inside a control.if branch, inside a control.while body), WITH ONE HARD REQUIREMENT: at least one real, non-control action (movement/combat/posture/sound - anything that actually does something, not timing.wait or memory.store_dark_location) must already have run earlier in this same plan first. This is engine-enforced, not just a guideline - a re_evaluate placed before any real action has run is silently skipped as a no-op and the plan just continues past it, wasting the step. Use it to check whether something ALREADY TRIED is actually working - e.g. put it right after a posture.stare to see if the stare is landing or the player is drifting away, or partway through a chase that's dragging on - not to immediately second-guess a plan that was just handed to you before anything in it has happened. Use it when whatever the original plan committed to no longer fits what's actually happening: the player left, got obstructed by geometry, the same beat has been held too long with nothing changing, or the situation has just genuinely moved on since the plan was written - rather than trying to force the rest of the original plan through regardless. When this runs, the engine gathers a completely fresh read of the current situation (the same kind of context this whole request already received, current position/torch counts/history included) PLUS a log of every step that has actually run so far this engagement and how long each one took, and asks for a new sub-plan. That sub-plan's own 'plan'/'despawn_band'/'global_rules' fully replace whatever was left of the original - not merged, a clean continuation from here. Not a substitute for ordinary control.if/control.while branching (which is free, instant, no LLM round trip) - this is for when the plan itself, not just one branch of it, needs to change; don't reach for it reflexively on every step, only when something has actually gone stale enough to be worth a real reconsideration.

control_if.description: CONTROL branch: evaluate 'condition' once, at the point this step is reached in plan execution, and run 'then' if true, otherwise 'else' (if given). Example: if the player isn't looking, take a step closer; otherwise hold.

else.description: Set this to null if there's nothing to do on the false branch - not every control.if needs an else.

control_while.description: CONTROL branch: repeat 'body' in a loop as long as 'condition' holds (re-checked between each iteration by the engine). Example: 'stalk the player while they are not looking at us' = while(not(predicate.player_looking_at_self)) { movement.approach }. 'max_iterations' is a mandatory safety cap - the engine still stops the loop after that many iterations even if the condition never flips, so a stuck predicate can't hang the entity forever without a new decision turn.

max_iterations.description: Semantic iteration cap - engine maps to a real bound (e.g. few=~3, some=~8, many=~20), not an exact count.

predicate.description: A boolean fact the engine evaluates on demand - the model picks which fact to check, never computes the answer itself. Compound predicates (not/and/or) wrap only simple predicates, one level deep, to keep the condition tree shallow and reliable for a small model to produce.

predicate_player_looking_at_self.description: True if the player currently has line of sight to / is facing the wendigo (Enderman-style stare detection), within the given angular band.

band.description: How directly the player has to be facing the wendigo to count, widest to narrowest: corner_of_eye (~60 degrees - about as wide as it can go before it's no longer plausibly visible in normal FOV at all), in_view (~30 degrees - actually looking toward it, not just able to see it peripherally), dead_stare (~10 degrees - looking almost dead at it). Pick corner_of_eye for 'notices something's off but hasn't focused on it yet', dead_stare for 'is definitely staring right at me'.

predicate_player_approaching.description: True once the player has closed at least this much of the distance between them and the wendigo, measured relative to however far apart they were the moment the CURRENTLY-RUNNING control.while loop started (that distance is captured once, fresh, each time a control.while begins - capped at 18 blocks, so a loop that started very far away doesn't need an unrealistic amount of closing to trigger). low/medium/high are relative thresholds scaled to that starting distance (roughly 22%/44%/67% of it), not fixed block counts, so this behaves consistently whether the loop started 6 blocks away or 18. Prefer this over predicate.player_distance for a 'break once they've closed in meaningfully during this loop' condition: a fixed absolute distance can already be satisfied or violated by whatever step ran right before the loop started (e.g. the wendigo's own movement.approach_band closing distance on its way in), which this avoids since it only measures change from the moment the loop itself began. Only meaningful inside a control.while - used inside control.if or a global_rule (neither of which loop) it always reads as though nothing has been covered yet.

band.description: How much of the loop-start distance counts as 'closed in' - low is a small amount of ground covered, high is most of it.

predicate_player_undetected.description: True as long as the wendigo is still safely unnoticed: the player is NOT looking at it within the given band, AND the player has NOT closed in by approach_band's amount since the current control.while loop started (see predicate.player_approaching for exactly what that measures - the negation is baked in here so composing it yourself isn't necessary). This is the single check for a 'stay hidden and keep creeping closer' loop (control.while(predicate.player_undetected(...)) { movement.approach_band(close) } then control.despawn/combat.lunge_attack once the loop ends) - prefer this over hand-building predicate.and(predicate.not(predicate.player_looking_at_self), predicate.not(predicate.player_approaching)) for that exact idiom, since manually composing a double negation is easy to get backwards (predicate.and(player_looking_at_self, player_approaching) looks similar but means the opposite: 'only keep going once already spotted and already closing in', which is false the instant the wendigo spawns unseen, so the loop runs zero times and immediately falls through to whatever comes next).

band.description: The player must NOT be looking at the wendigo within this angular band for it to still count as undetected - same bands as predicate.player_looking_at_self.

approach_band.description: The player must NOT have closed in by this much since the current control.while loop started for it to still count as undetected - same relative bands as predicate.player_approaching (low = a small amount of ground closed already breaks it, high = tolerates them closing in quite a lot before it breaks).

predicate_self_in_darkness.description: True if the wendigo's current position is dark enough to be considered hidden.

predicate_player_in_darkness.description: True if the player's current position is dark enough to be considered hidden.

predicate_player_near_light_edge.description: True if the player is near the boundary between a lit and dark area (e.g. at the edge of a torch's light radius) - useful for deciding whether to wait for them to cross into darkness rather than approaching now.

predicate_dark_location_stored.description: True if a memory.store_dark_location step has stored a spot that's still considered valid (not yet consumed/invalidated).

predicate_player_distance.description: Compares the player's current distance against a semantic band. While attached to a wall/ceiling with the player somewhere below (within about 30 blocks straight down), 'distance' here means horizontal distance down that same vertical column, not the raw diagonal - a wendigo hanging directly above the player already reads as grab_distance even from well overhead, since a movement.drop is what actually closes that gap, not a walk. This is exactly what makes control.while(farther_than lunge_distance){movement.hold} then combat.lunge_attack work while perched on a ceiling: it resolves the instant the player walks underneath, not once they've somehow closed the full diagonal distance.

distance.description: Shared proximity ladder, nearest to furthest: grab_distance (~0-4 blocks, melee/strike range), lunge_distance (~5-9, the range to commit to combat.lunge_attack from), close_quarters (~10-14), medium (~15-24), far (~25+). These are the same bands used to label each scanned spot's distance in the prompt, so you can tell before committing to spawn_at whether a spot is already inside combat/flee range of the player - e.g. control.while(farther_than lunge_distance){movement.hold} then combat.lunge_attack to wait for the player to close in before committing, rather than lunging from too far away or walking straight at them the whole way in, or closer_than close_quarters to decide it's time to retreat. Works from a wall/ceiling perch too (see this predicate's own top-level description on the cylinder distance) - waiting at lunge_distance while attached above a patrol route, then dropping (movement.drop) straight into combat.lunge_attack or combat.chase the instant they walk underneath, is a strong, patient use of this pattern, not just a ground-level one.

predicate_player_unreachable.description: True if the wendigo's most recent movement action couldn't find or maintain a path to its target (e.g. the player is behind a sealed wall, or across a gap it can't cross). Useful for giving up and retreating instead of holding forever.

predicate_target_moving.description: True if the player currently has real horizontal velocity - walking, running, or sneaking all count, standing still (even mid-jump, even sprint-stopped a moment ago) doesn't. False if there's no player to check at all, same as most other player-facing predicates here. Use this to gate a control.while(target_moving) { movement.approach... } loop - keep tailing them only as long as they're actually on the move - or as a control.if condition to branch behavior on whether they're currently walking or holding still. See predicate.target_is_stopped for the complementary case.

predicate_target_is_stopped.description: True if the player currently has no real horizontal velocity - genuinely standing still, not merely between two steps. NOT simply the logical negation of predicate.target_moving: with no player to check, both read false rather than one reading true - there's nothing to be 'stopped' if there's no target at all. Use this to branch toward a held stare/ambush the instant the player plants themselves (e.g. control.if(target_is_stopped) { posture.stare... }) as a natural pair with predicate.target_moving's own follow-while-moving idiom.

predicate_and.description: True only if both operand predicates are true.

predicate_or.description: True if either operand predicate is true.
